paper_title: MemSteer: Turning User Histories into Supervision for Agent Memory Optimization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: An effective agent memory system should adapt to a user's history and task requirements. Human-annotated supervision can guide this adaptation by providing feedback for evaluating and improving memory designs. Yet suitable labels are rarely available for new user histories, and manually constructing QA pairs and supporting evidence is costly. We introduce MemSteer, which turns unlabeled user histories into question-answer (QA) supervision with supporting evidence for memory-design optimization. MemSteer constructs an evidence-grounded answer plan that specifies how facts across related records jointly support a reference answer. The plan guides question generation, while source-grounded auditing and blind answer recovery check the resulting annotations. To study the utility of this supervision, we develop MemSteer-Opt, which combines QA-based design evaluation with evidence-guided failure diagnosis to revise memory store, retrieval, and context construction without updating model parameters. Experiments on ATM-Bench and RHELM show that this supervision is competitive with official-QA-guided optimization. Relative to Base-BM25, MemSteer-Opt improves ATM-Bench Question Score by 13.4 points and RHELM accuracy by 4.1 and 6.6 points without and with external data, respectively. The supervision also benefits two existing optimizers on ATM-Bench, while new-user experiments demonstrate continued design optimization using supervision generated from the target histories.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Agents that assist users over time need to draw on information accumulated across conversations, emails, and documents. An external memory system supports this process by storing and organizing the users history and retrieving relevant context for the agent. Storage granularity, retrieval strategy, and answer-context construction shape how effectively the agent can use that history. User histories differ in their content, modalities, and organization, so memory design effective for one user may be less suitable for another. This motivates adapting memory designs to user histories. Recent methods such as MemEvolve, ALMA, and optimize memory designs using downstream task feedback (Zhang et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026). While executable tasks can provide feedback through their outcomes, personal records and interactions often lack an explicit signal for assessing memory quality. Annotated questionanswer (QA) pairs can Work done during an internship at MSRA. 1 Figure 1: Motivation for MemSteer. User histories vary in data characteristics, so one memory design may not suit every user. Automatic design adaptation through iterative optimization requires feedback on memory performance. MemSteer supports this optimization by automatically generating QAevidence supervision from unlabeled histories, avoiding laborintensive manual labeling.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: supply this signal (Pan et al., 2026), but constructing questions, reference answers, and supporting evidence for each new history is costly. This motivates our question (Figure 1): Can unlabeled user histories guide memory-design optimization? Generating QA from the history itself offers potential source of this feedback. Within agent memory, MemBuilder uses synthetic QA rewards to train memory-construction policies (Shen et al., 2026), while MemMA uses QA probes to repair stored memories (Lin et al., 2026). We instead investigate whether history-derived QA can provide reliable feedback for evaluating and improving memory-system designs. For memory-design optimization, reference answers determine how candidate designs are evaluated, while source evidence can help diagnose unsuccessful responses. Unsupported answers or mismatched evidence can misdirect design selection and later revisions. We propose MemSteer, framework that turns unlabeled user histories into source-grounded QA evidence supervision for memory-design optimization (Figure 2). It brings together related source records and specifies how their facts jointly support reference answer. The resulting evidencegrounded answer plan guides question generation. Source-grounded auditing checks the generated QA for evidence support and consistency, while blind answer recovery assesses whether the reference answer can be recovered from the sampled records. To investigate the utility of MemSteers generated supervision, we develop MemSteer-Opt, an evidence-guided memory-design optimizer. It uses source evidence and execution traces to identify whether incorrect responses stem from storage, retrieval, or answer generation, then proposes targeted design revisions and evaluates them using QA performance. Starting from basic memory system, we use MemSteer-Opt to optimize memory representations, retrieval strategies, and context construction. We further supply the generated QA to and MemEvolve (Pan et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025), allowing each framework to optimize within its own design space. Our contributions are threefold: Memory-design optimization from unlabeled histories. MemSteer constructs QAevidence supervision from unlabeled user histories for evaluating and improving memory designs without updating model parameters. Evidence-grounded answer planning and verification. We construct answer plans that make explicit how source facts jointly support reference answer for question generation. Sourcegrounded verification checks the resulting annotations. Empirical validation across optimizers and user histories. Experiments with MemSteer-Opt on ATM-Bench and RHELM (Mei et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026) show that generated supervision improves memory designs and is competitive with the Official-QA reference. Further experiments demonstrate its utility for two existing optimizers on ATM-Bench and for continued optimization on new user histories.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Memory-design optimization. Applications differ in what agents need to remember and how they use past information, making memory design an application-specific engineering challenge (Xiong et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026). Recent work therefore explores automatic memory-design optimization to accommodate these requirements while reducing reliance on manual design. ALMA searches over code-based memory designs using task success and interaction logs as feedback (Xiong et al., 2026). MemEvolve introduces dual-level process that evolves both experience memory and its underlying architecture (Zhang et al., 2025). searches over memory programs by jointly refining their schema, logic, and instructions through task feedback and reflective code evolution (Pan et al., 2026). At narrower level, CluE refines memory-extraction prompts using downstream feedback across heterogeneous tasks (Yang et al., 2026). These methods optimize memory designs using feedback from downstream tasks. In many personal-memory applications, however, user records and everyday interactions do not naturally yield success-or-failure signals to guide memory-design optimization. We therefore investigate how these histories can be turned into supervision for memorydesign optimization. Synthetic queries and QA for training and evaluation. Outside agent memory, synthetic data has been used to reduce annotation requirements for model training and system evaluation. Promp-

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: tagator generates querydocument pairs to train task-specific dense retrievers (Dai et al., 2022). Alberti et al. (2019) generate QA by selecting answers, formulating questions, and filtering pairs through answer-recovery consistency before training reading-comprehension models. For structured synthesis, GraphGen samples knowledge-graph subgraphs to construct atomic, aggregated, and multi-hop QA for supervised fine-tuning (Chen et al., 2025). For evaluation, DataMorgana constructs corpus-specific RAG benchmarks with configurable user and question categories (Filice et al., 2025), while Ragas uses graph relationships to synthesize multi-hop test questions (Ragas, 2026). The usefulness of synthetic questions has also been studied directly: Yue et al. (2022) learn question value estimator to select examples that improve target-domain QA performance, rather than relying only on generation or answer-model scores. We ask whether synthetic QA can provide effective feedback for memory-design optimization. Synthetic supervision for agent memory. Generated QA has also been incorporated into memory learning and refinement. MemBuilder and CMI-Mem generate QA pairs from current sessions and retrieved memories, then use answering accuracy as reward signal to train LLMs to construct and update memories via reinforcement learning (Shen et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). MemMA generates QA probes from each session and its historical context, then uses answering failures to repair the memory bank (Lin et al., 2026). MemMA also examines how the choice of probe generator affects repair outcomes. MemSteer instead uses generated QA pairs with source-grounded evidence to guide memory-design optimization, rather than to train memory models or repair stored memories. This turns user histories into source of feedback for memory-design optimization without requiring manually annotated QA for the target history.

sections.title: 3.1 OVERVIEW
sections.content: Histories from different users vary in content and structure, so memory design effective for one user may be less suitable for another. Given unlabeled user histories H, our goal is to improve agent memory designs without manually annotating QA pairs for those histories. To this end, MemSteer constructs QAevidence supervision: DH = {(qi, ai, Ei)}N i=1, (1) where qi is question about the history, ai is its reference answer, and Ei identifies the selected source records, with source-span citations providing provenance for the supporting facts. Reference answers provide criterion for evaluating memory designs, while evidence annotations support the diagnosis of unsuccessful responses. We describe the supervision construction process in Section 3.2. To assess the effectiveness of this supervision for memory-design optimization, we develop MemSteer-Opt, which evaluates candidate designs and uses evidence-guided feedback to propose iterative revisions (Section 3.3). The generated supervision can also be supplied to existing optimizers, allowing each to retain its own design space and optimization procedure.

sections.title: 3.2 CONSTRUCTING QA–EVIDENCE SUPERVISION
sections.content: MemSteer constructs QAevidence annotations by selecting related source records, establishing how their facts support an answer, and generating and verifying the corresponding question. Graph-guided material preparation. We organize each users history as graph of source records, preserving original text, identifiers, and source-provided structural metadata. Edges connect records sharing conversation, occupying adjacent document sections, explicitly referencing one another, or having sufficient lexical overlap. Path-based expansion from seed samples connected subgraph, whose records form context-budgeted material bundle with source-span references for identifying jointly supporting facts and evidence records. Evidence-grounded answer planning and question generation. Given material bundle B, an LLM-based planner constructs an evidence-grounded answer plan that specifies what the question

We verify each candidate through semantic audit followed by blind answer recovery. Normalization rules are detailed in Appendix A.4. We partition the generated QAevidence annotations into disjoint training and validation sets, using the former to generate revision proposals and the latter to select memory designs.

sections.title: 3.3 MEMSTEER-OPT: EVIDENCE-GUIDED MEMORY-DESIGN OPTIMIZATION
sections.content: MemSteer-Opt uses the generated QAevidence supervision to evaluate memory designs and turn observed failures into feedback for iterative revisions. Design space and evaluation. Starting from basic memory system, MemSteer-Opt iteratively optimizes how historical records are organized into memory units and indexed, how relevant records are retrieved, and how retrieved records are assembled into the context supplied to the answerer. We represent these storage, retrieval, and context-construction choices as memory design = (s, r, c). Under design d, the system constructs memory Md from the users historical records H: Md = Stores(H). For each question qi, it retrieves information from Md, assembles the answer context Xd,i, and generates response ˆad,i: Xd,i = Contextc(Retriever(qi, Md)), ˆad,i = Answer(qi, Xd,i). (2) We evaluate each prediction ˆad,i against its reference answer ai under fixed scoring protocol, yielding binary correctness score yd,i {0, 1}. We score design by its accuracy on the same validation set as A(d) = 1 i=1 yd,i, where Nval is the number of validation questions. We use Nval this binary validation accuracy for design selection; final benchmark scores follow the corresponding evaluation protocols (Appendix A.4). We hold the answering model, its instruction prompt, and the final context budget fixed across designs. (cid:80)Nval Evidence-guided diagnosis and sampling. Beyond scoring candidate designs, we use the automatically constructed evidence annotations to build targeted feedback for revising memory designs. (i) Evidence-guided diagnosis. For each incorrect training-set response, we use its evidence annotations to check whether the required source records and cited passages are fully available in the final answer context. If so, we label an answering failure. For missing evidence, we use the annotated source IDs to check whether the current memory system can recover the corresponding records. We assign storage failure if any missing record is unrecoverable, and retrieval failure if all missing records are recoverable. (ii) Failure-stratified sampling. To cover different failure modes within the proposers input-context budget, we sample cases separately from each observed failure category. Each sampled case includes the question, its reference answer and annotated source evidence, together with the current systems response and diagnostic results. Together with the current design and revision history, these cases form the input to the design proposer. Feedback-guided revision and selection. Given this feedback, an LLM-based design proposer proposes revised design d, using the diagnosed failures to guide changes to storage, retrieval, or context construction. It also provides rationale for the proposed changes. We rebuild the memory under each valid candidate and evaluate its accuracy on the fixed validation set. We replace the current design dt with only if A(d) > A(dt); otherwise, we retain dt. After accepting revision, we rerun the updated system on the training set to refresh the failure diagnoses and sampled feedback for the next iteration. Supervision for existing memory-design optimizers. Beyond MemSteer-Opt, we use the generated supervision to guide existing memory-design optimizers within their own design spaces. Generated questions and reference answers supply task feedback for evaluating and refining memory designs; source evidence can additionally support feedback when the optimizers interface accommodates it. This tests whether the supervision remains useful across optimization frameworks.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We address four questions: Q1 (4.2): Can generated supervision guide memory-design optimization? Q2 (4.3): Can optimized memory designs transfer and adapt? Q3 (4.4): Which supervisionconstruction choices matter? Q4 (4.5): Does evidence-guided feedback improve optimization?

sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Benchmarks and evaluation. ATM-Bench (Mei et al., 2026b) is multimodal personal-memory QA benchmark built from approximately four years of personal records. Its corpus contains 11,034 email, image, and video records. Unless otherwise specified, we follow the ATM-Bench scoring protocol and evaluate performance on its 1,013-question main set and 31-question hard multi-hop set. RHELM (Zhang et al., 2026) covers 21,142 interaction records from ten personas, evaluated with and without external data sources. Benchmark selection is discussed in Appendix A.1. Optimizers and protocol. MemSteer-Opt starts from basic record-level retrieve-and-read system, which we refer to as Base-BM25: it indexes source text and metadata and uses the original question for BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009) retrieval. Retrieved content is assembled in ranked order within fixed context budget and passed to fixed answering model. (Pan et al., 2026) and MemEvolve (Zhang et al., 2025) retain their own starting systems and design spaces. MemSteer uses our generated QAevidence supervision for both training and validation while official QA is used only for testing. MemSteer-Opt runs 20 reflective evolution iterations per setting. Models and metrics. On ATM-Bench, DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) serves as the answerer, open-answer judge (Zheng et al., 2023), and design proposer, matching the answerer and judge used by the corresponding leaderboard configurations (Mei et al., 2026a). We report Question Score (QS) and evidence recall at 10 (R@10). On RHELM, we follow the official protocol, using GPT-4.1-mini (OpenAI, 2025) for answering and evaluation and reporting overall accuracy, separately with and without external data. We include existing memory systems as performance references; their configurations and additional results are detailed in Appendix A.2 and Appendix B.3.

sections.title: 4.2 CAN GENERATED SUPERVISION GUIDE MEMORY-DESIGN OPTIMIZATION?
sections.content: Tables 1 and 2 compare MemSteer-generated supervision with official annotations (Official-QA) on ATM-Bench and RHELM; the ATM comparison also includes two external optimizers. OfficialQA uses 600 of the 1,013 official ATM items and 788 of the 1,305 RHELM items for training and validation. These items remain in its evaluation sets, whereas MemSteer uses no evaluation items for training. The final RHELM MemSteer configuration uses 788 generated training items and is evaluated on all 1,305 official QA items. Based on Tables 1 and 2, we make the following observations. Generated supervision improves memory designs. With MemSteer supervision, MemSteer-Opt raises QS from 54.9 to 68.3 on ATM-Bench and from 8.2 to 29.1 on Hard, alongside gains in evidence recall  (Table 1)  . On RHELM, MemSteer improves over Base-BM25 by 4.1 accuracy points without external data and 6.6 points with it  (Table 2)  . Generated supervision is competitive with the human-annotated reference. On ATM-Bench, MemSteer scores marginally higher than Official-QA across all four metrics, including QS margins of 1.1 points on the main set and 1.3 points on Hard. On RHELM, MemSteer remains 0.1 and 0.8 accuracy points below Official-QA without and with external data, respectively. The supervision also benefits existing optimizers. From their own starting systems, and MemEvolve gain 6.0 and 18.6 main-set QS points with MemSteer supervision, compared with 4.4 and 18.6 points with Official-QA. Thus, the supervisions utility is not limited to MemSteer-Opt. The benefit is not uniform: on Hard, MemEvolve obtains smaller gains than with Official-QA, and its R@10 decreases by 0.1 points. The optimized designs are competitive with existing memory systems. On ATM-Bench, MemSteer-Opt achieves the highest QS among the non-oracle systems using DeepSeek-V4 as the answerer. On RHELM with external data, MemSteer reaches 39.9 accuracy, compared with 33.9 for the strongest listed RAG, long-context, or memory-system baseline. Without external data, it remains competitive with the strongest listed baseline, RAG with k=50.

sections.title: 4.3 CAN OPTIMIZED MEMORY DESIGNS TRANSFER AND ADAPT?
sections.content: We test design reuse across benchmarks and continued optimization for users, respectively. Cross-benchmark transfer. We freeze the design optimized with generated ATM-Bench QA and apply it to RHELM records without target-domain optimization. ATM-Bench-evolved(frozen) outperforms Base-BM25 by 4.1 and 5.3 accuracy points without and with external data, respectively  (Table 2)  . These results suggest that some of the design improvements learned on ATM-Bench remain useful on RHELM without target-domain optimization. When further optimized using either RHELM Official-QA or QA generated from RHELM histories, the transferred design achieves further gains. Generated supervision achieves performance close to the Official-QA reference without requiring manually annotated target-domain QA for optimization. Cross-user transfer and continuation. We apply frozen design optimized on six RHELM users to Martin Keller and David R. Ellis, who are excluded from the sourceuser pool. We then continue optimization from this shared design using QAevidence supervision generated from each target users history, reserving official QA for evaluation (Appendix A.3). sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Training-question budget. Increasing the budget from 100 to 200 questions yields the largest performance gains in the evaluated sweep. Beyond 200, retrieval recall largely plateaus, while QS improves overall on both ATM-Bench and ATM-Bench-Hard (Appendix B.2).

sections.title: 4.5 DOES EVIDENCE-GUIDED FEEDBACK IMPROVE OPTIMIZATION?
sections.content: We test whether explicit failure diagnosis improves on raw-evidence feedback and whether failurestratified sampling further improves memory-design optimization. All four feedback conditions use MemSteer-generated QAevidence supervision and start from Base-BM25 (Figure 3). Figure 3: Attribution and sampling ablation on ATM-Bench and ATM-Bench-Hard. Bars report QS and R@10 (%). Optimized conditions use MemSteer-generated supervision and start from BaseBM25; Diagnosis + stratified sampling is the full MemSteer-Opt configuration. We compare four ways to construct feedback from unsuccessful cases. Random-30 randomly samples up to 30 scored failures per round and gives the design proposer their questions, reference answers, predictions, scores, retrieval traces, and answer-context excerpts. Random-30 + Gold evidence retains the random sampling and adds required-evidence IDs and gold-record excerpts, but no failure attribution. Random-30 + Diagnosis further adds evidence-grounded failure attribution while retaining random sampling. Diagnosis + stratified sampling (ours) keeps the diagnostic feedback and samples up to ten cases per failure category, preventing frequent failure types from exhausting the feedback budget. Appendix A.5 details the feedback fields, while Appendix B.5 shows an accepted architectural trajectory. We make the following observations. (i) Adding gold evidence provides only limited improvement over trace-based feedback. (ii) Explicit failure attribution yields larger gains, particularly in evidence retrieval, supporting the use of stage-level diagnostic feedback rather than raw evidence alone. (iii) Combining diagnosis with stratified sampling achieves the highest downstream QS, although diagnosis with random sampling yields higher evidence recall on Hard.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented MemSteer, framework for constructing QAevidence supervision from unlabeled user histories and using it to guide memory-design optimization. Rather than requiring manually annotated QA for each new history, MemSteer derives reference answers and supporting evidence from the records themselves. These annotations serve complementary purposes: reference answers support the evaluation of candidate memory designs, while source evidence helps diagnose unsuccessful responses and guide revisions. We instantiate this approach in MemSteer-Opt and also use the generated supervision with existing optimizers that retain their own design spaces. Experiments on ATM-Bench and RHELM show that generated supervision improves memory designs, achieves performance competitive with the Official-QA reference, and supports continued adaptation to new user histories.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: Our experiments use released benchmark data under their published terms, without collecting new personal data or conducting human-subjects studies. Source records are processed through thirdparty LLM APIs, and generated QA may reveal sensitive information by combining facts across records. Deployment on personal histories should therefore require informed user consent and appropriate privacy safeguards. MemSteer is intended to improve memory systems for users, not to enable unauthorized profiling.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: Section 3.2 specifies the supervision-construction pipeline (graph-guided material preparation, evidence-grounded answer planning, question generation, and source-grounded verification), and Section 3.3 specifies the design space, evaluation protocol, evidence-guided diagnosis, and acceptance rule of MemSteer-Opt. Section 4.1 describes the benchmarks, baselines, iteration budget, and model roles. Appendix documents additional experimental details, including evaluation populations and feedback inputs; Appendix reports further experimental results. Because the pipeline depends on remote LLM APIs, exact outputs may vary with model nondeterminism and provider updates; we therefore report the model identities used for each role.

sections.title: LLM USAGE
sections.content: LLMs perform evidence-grounded answer planning, question generation, source-grounded auditing, and blind answer recovery in MemSteer. They also propose design revisions in MemSteer-Opt, act as fixed answerers and answer judges, and perform shared filtering and post hoc QA-quality evaluation. We use DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1, and GPT-5-mini across these roles (Section 4.1). In preparing this paper, we also used LLM assistants for language editing and coding assistance. The authors reviewed all such output and take full responsibility for this paper.

sections.title: A ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 BENCHMARK SELECTION We prioritize ATM-Bench (Mei et al., 2026b) and RHELM (Zhang et al., 2026) because recent work characterizes performance on LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) and LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2024) as near-saturated in conversational-memory QA settings (He et al., 2026). ATM-Bench combines real-world images, videos, and emails, whereas RHELM couples evolving simulated user dialogues with external textual sources such as emails and documents. A.2 REFERENCE SYSTEMS Table 1 compares DeepSeek-V4-based Memexa (labazhou2024, 2026), A-Mem (Xu et al., 2025), MemPalace (MemPalace, 2026), and HippoRAG2 (Gutierrez et al., 2025) on ATM-Bench (Mei et al., 2026a). Table 2 includes the RHELM reference results (Zhang et al., 2026) for RAG (k {20, 50}), Hybrid (k {5, 20, 50}), MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023), Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), and MemU (NevaMind AI, 2025), all using GPT-4.1-mini as the answering model. Hybrid combines dense retrieval with BM25 through reciprocal rank fusion. The same table reports 1M-context inference with Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite (Comanici et al., 2025), Qwen-2.5-14B-Instruct (1M) (Yang et al., 2025), and GPT-4.1-mini (OpenAI, 2025). The Base-BM25, optimized, and transferred-design rows follow the protocols in Sections 4.1 and 4.3. Appendix Table 8 additionally reports RAG with GPT-4.1 (OpenAI, 2025), Gemini-2.5-Pro (Comanici et al., 2025), and Claude-Opus-4.5 (Anthropic, 2025), all at = 20. Native Qwen3-VL/GPT-5-mini results, including ATM-RAG (Mei et al., 2026b), Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2023), ScrapMem (Chang & Ren, 2026), and MemoryOS (Kang et al., 2025), are included in Appendix Table 7. A.3 EVALUATION POPULATIONS The training split drives failure attribution and revision proposals, whereas validation is used to accept revisions and select the final design. MemSteer uses generated QAevidence supervision for these processes, without using benchmark evaluation questions. The Official-QA reference instead uses official QA for training and validation; these items remain included in evaluation. On ATM-Bench, both the Official-QA and MemSteer conditions use 400 training items and fixed 200-item validation set; the former uses official QA and the latter uses QAevidence supervision generated from the records. Evaluation covers all 1,013 official QA items, including the 600 items used for Official-QA training and validation. ATM-Bench-Hard, the 31-question hard multi-hop subset, is reported separately. Leaderboard references also use the full 1,013-item population. RHELM contains 1,305 official QA items from ten personas and is evaluated on the full official set, both with and without external data sources. The Official-QA reference uses 524 official items for training and 264 for validation; these items remain included in evaluation. The final MemSteer configuration uses 788 generated QAevidence items for training, without using official QA for training or design selection. In the six-user setting, four personas provide training supervision, two provide validation supervision, and the remaining four are held out  (Table 9)  . For personal continuation, MemSteer generates 421 supervision items from Martin Kellers history, split into 282 training and 139 validation items, and evaluates the continued design on 228 official questions. For David R. Ellis, it generates 337 supervision items, split into 223 training and 114 validation items, and evaluates on 158 official questions. A.4 EVALUATION METRICS On ATM-Bench, Question Score (QS) uses exact match for numerical items, Jaccard partial credit for list items, and judge scores for open-ended items. R@10 averages the fraction of gold evidence records among the top-10 retrieved records over questions. Blind answer agreement. Blind answer recovery checks type-normalized exact agreement: normalized text equality, set equality for lists, and exact value-and-unit agreement for numerical answers.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Boolean answers are matched exactly. Evidence coverage is checked at the record level, requiring citations to every selected evidence record. Design-selection accuracy. Validation accuracy guides revision acceptance and design selection. Predictions identical to their reference answers are scored as correct; other responses receive binary correctness judgment from fixed LLM judge. Final ATM-Bench evaluation uses Question Score (QS), which includes partial credit for list questions. Final RHELM evaluation reports overall accuracy, computed as the mean of binary correctness judgments from the official evaluator. A.5 FEEDBACK INPUTS Gold evidence denotes the reference source evidence in MemSteer-generated QAevidence supervision, not human-annotated evidence. For Random-30, each sampled case includes the question, reference answer, prediction and score, ranked retrieved-record IDs, IDs actually delivered to the answer. Gold evidence remains unmarked in Random-30, even if it appears in the context. Random30 + Gold evidence adds required-evidence IDs and gold-record excerpts without programmatic failure attribution. Random-30 + Diagnosis retains random sampling and additionally provides failure-stage labels, missing-evidence IDs, evidence checks, and memory-lookup results. Diagnosis + stratified sampling uses the same diagnostic information but organizes examples by failure category before allocating the feedback budget.

In the six-user setting, four personas provide training supervision and two provide validation supervision; the remaining four are held out from optimization. In the ten-user setting, all personas participate in optimization. OfficialQA uses 40% of each personas official QA for training and 20% for validation, whereas MemSteer uses QAevidence supervision generated from user histories and reserves official QA for evaluation.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Transfer of the six-user shared design. Table 9(a) shows that the shared design improves pooled accuracy on the six source users from 31.5% to 34.3%. However, this improvement does not carry over in aggregate to the four users held out from optimization. These results highlight heterogeneous transfer across users: design optimized on the source users does not necessarily benefit other users. This makes the target-user continuation valuable, as studied in Table 3. Generated versus official supervision in the ten-user setting. Table 9(b) shows that MemSteer improves over Base-BM25 for all ten personas, raising pooled accuracy from 33.3% to 39.9%. Its overall accuracy is 0.8 points below the 40.7% obtained with Official-QA supervision. Note that MemSteer reserves official QA for evaluation, whereas the Official-QA results include questions used for training or validation. Thus, history-generated supervision provides an effective alternative for optimizing shared memory design without relying on official QA for training or design selection. B.5 EXAMPLE ACCEPTED ARCHITECTURE TRAJECTORY Figure 5: Accepted memory-design optimization trajectory on ATM-Bench, starting from BaseBM25 and comprising nine accepted revisions. Numbered badges and colored arrows indicate the revision order. Figure 5 traces one accepted memory-design optimization trajectory on ATM-Bench. Starting from Base-BM25 with raw queries and direct reader, revisions add BGE-M3 (Chen et al., 2024) dense retrieval; hybrid retrieval with BGE reranking; question decomposition; HyDE (Gao et al., 2023) and second retrieval stage; HyDE queries; 180-candidate pool with 90 reranked items; and answer verification. The final design uses four HyDE queries, reranks 120 candidates, reads 25 records, and permits 4,000-token output. The sequence moves from retrieval representation and ranking to multi-query context construction and answer validation.

sections.title: C LIMITATIONS
sections.content: MemSteers supervision is generated and verified by LLMs without human certification, so errors or biases shared across answer planning, source-grounded auditing, and blind answer recovery can pass verification undetected. Blind answer recovery checks whether the reference answer is recoverable from the sampled records and every selected evidence record is cited; it does not establish that each record is necessary. Generated questions follow the distribution of the history rather than users actual information needs. MemSteer-Opt explores constrained, largely retrieval-centric design space. Finally, our evaluation covers two benchmarks, one of which (RHELM) consists of synthetic personas, so evidence on real, heterogeneous user histories remains limited.
